subject: religious-studies
topicDisplay: Religious & Ethical Teachings about Medical Ethics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What is meant by the "sanctity of life"?
options: The belief that life is holy and God-given
The belief that life has no real value
The belief that only human success matters
The belief that life may be ended freely
questions.explain: Sanctity of life means life is sacred because it is created and given by God.

questions.q: The Christian teaching that humans are made "in the image of God" (imago Dei) suggests that:
options: Human life is uniquely valuable and should be respected
Humans look physically identical to God
Only Christians are created by God
Human life has no special status
questions.explain: Being made in God's image (Genesis 1:27) gives human life a special, sacred value.

questions.q: The "quality of life" argument holds that:
options: The value of a life depends on its condition and wellbeing
All life is equally sacred whatever its condition
Only God can ever end a life
Life must always be preserved at any cost
questions.explain: Quality of life judges worth by wellbeing, and is often contrasted with the sanctity of life principle.

questions.q: Which of the Ten Commandments is most often linked to the sanctity of life?
questions.explain: "You shall not murder" (Exodus 20:13) upholds the sacredness of human life.

questions.q: The Qur'an teaches that "whoever saves a life, it is as if he saved all mankind." This shows that Islam:
options: Places great value on the sanctity of human life
Teaches that life belongs to humans alone
questions.explain: This verse (Qur'an 5:32) stresses that all human life is precious and given by Allah.

questions.q: When St Paul writes that "your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit," he is teaching Christians to:
options: Respect and care for their bodies
Reject all forms of medical treatment
questions.explain: This teaching (1 Corinthians 6:19) means the body is God-given and should be respected and cared for.

questions.q: In which year was the Abortion Act passed in the UK?
questions.explain: The 1967 Abortion Act legalised abortion in Great Britain under certain conditions.

questions.q: The general upper time limit for a legal abortion in Great Britain is:
questions.explain: The limit was set at 24 weeks by the Human Fertilisation and Embryology Act 1990.

questions.q: Someone who is "pro-choice" believes that:
options: A woman should have the right to decide about an abortion
Life begins at conception and must be protected
questions.explain: Pro-choice supporters argue that a woman has the right to control her own body.

questions.q: The Roman Catholic Church teaches that human life, and its full protection, begins at:
questions.explain: Catholic teaching holds that life begins at conception, so abortion is regarded as wrong.

questions.q: Many Muslim scholars teach that ensoulment (the soul entering the foetus) happens at around:
questions.explain: A common Islamic teaching, based on hadith, is that the soul enters the foetus at about 120 days.

questions.q: In the UK, a doctor who deliberately gives a lethal injection to end a patient's life could be charged with:
options: No offence, as it is legal
questions.explain: Active euthanasia is illegal in the UK and treated as murder or manslaughter.

questions.q: "Voluntary euthanasia" means that:
options: A person's life is ended at their own request
A person is killed against their wishes
A person dies of natural causes
questions.explain: Voluntary euthanasia is carried out at the clear request of the person concerned.

questions.q: A Christian who strongly believes in the sanctity of life is asked by a dying relative to help end their suffering. They are most likely to:
options: Refuse and support hospice or palliative care instead
Say that human life has no value
questions.explain: Belief in the sanctity of life usually leads to rejecting euthanasia in favour of palliative care.

questions.q: In fertility treatment, "IVF" stands for:
questions.explain: IVF (in vitro fertilisation) fertilises an egg with sperm in a laboratory.

questions.q: The world's first "test-tube baby," born through IVF in 1978, was:
questions.explain: Louise Brown, born in England in 1978, was the first baby conceived through IVF.

questions.q: Surrogacy is best described as:
options: A woman carrying and giving birth to a baby for another couple
Fertilising an egg in a laboratory dish
questions.explain: In surrogacy, one woman carries and delivers a child on behalf of another person or couple.

questions.q: A Catholic couple who cannot conceive ask their priest about IVF. He is most likely to:
options: Discourage it, partly because spare embryos may be destroyed
Strongly encourage it as a religious duty
Say the Church has no teaching on it
questions.explain: The Catholic Church opposes IVF partly because unused embryos, seen as human life, may be discarded.

questions.q: "Genetic engineering" refers to:
options: Changing or manipulating the genes of a living organism
Carrying a baby for another couple
questions.explain: Genetic engineering involves altering an organism's genes, raising ethical questions for many believers.

questions.q: A couple use embryo screening to select an embryo whose stem cells could treat their seriously ill child. This selected child is known as a:
questions.explain: A saviour sibling is conceived and selected to provide compatible tissue or cells for a sick brother or sister.
